Your browser is a program on **your** computer. It can open files saved on that computer or ask a server on the internet for files. In both cases, the browser assembles the page that you see.

## Your personal computer is your first web workshop

A **personal computer** is the device in front of you: perhaps a laptop, desktop, or Chromebook. It stores files and runs programs. Two programs matter especially in this book:

- A **text editor** lets you write and save code as plain text.
- A **web browser**—such as Chrome, Edge, Firefox, or Safari—reads web files and shows a page.

When your browser is doing the work on your device, your device is called the **client**. “Client” does not mean a different kind of computer. It means the computer that asks for a page and uses it.

For the first pages in this book, the client is all you need. You will save a file, open it in your browser, edit it, save again, and refresh the page to see the change.

## Keep each website in its own folder

A website is a group of related files. Make one folder for one project so its files stay together. For the next chapter, create a folder named `my-game-site` with these two files inside it:

```
my-game-site/
  index.html
  styles.css
```

`index.html` will describe the page. `styles.css` will describe its colors, spacing, and layout. The endings after the dots are part of the file names:

- `.html` means an HTML page.
- `.css` means a CSS style sheet.
- `.js` will later mean a JavaScript program.

Be careful to save plain-text files with the right ending. A file named `index.html.txt` is a text document, not a web page. If you cannot see file endings, ask a teacher or an adult to help turn them on.

## The browser turns files into a page

When you open `index.html`, the browser reads the HTML instructions and creates the page. If the HTML links to `styles.css`, the browser reads that file too. It uses CSS to decide how the same page should look.

Think of the jobs this way:

| Tool or file | Main job | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| HTML | structure and meaning | a heading, a paragraph, a button |
| CSS | appearance and layout | a blue button, a roomy card, a centered title |
| JavaScript | behavior that changes | what happens after a player clicks |

HTML and CSS can make a useful, polished **static website**. “Static” means that the page does not yet run its own rules or change itself. A button can look like a game button before it has JavaScript to react to a click.

## Local files and web addresses

You can open a saved file directly from your computer. Its address often begins with `file:///`. For example, it might look similar to this:

```
file:///Users/your-name/Documents/my-game-site/index.html
```

This address means, “Browser, open this file from this computer.” It does not put your page on the internet.

An internet address usually begins with `https://`, such as `https://example.com`. That tells the browser to contact a **server**. A server is a computer program that keeps web files ready and sends a requested file back to a browser.

::: {.callout-note .advanced-study title="A browser request, step by step" icon="false" collapse="false"}

[OPTIONAL DEEPER DIVE]{.study-badge}

When you visit an internet address, the browser first finds the server for that address. Then it sends a **request**, such as “Please send the home page.” The server sends a **response**, such as the HTML file. The browser may make more requests for the page's CSS, pictures, fonts, or JavaScript.

The server supplies files; the browser on the client turns them into the page. A later game might ask a server for an image or level file, but its drawing and player controls can still run in the browser.

:::

## Two kinds of servers you will meet

A public server is connected to the internet so many people can visit a website. We will not publish anything in this book.

A **local server** runs only on your own computer. It gives files an address such as `http://127.0.0.1:8000/`. `127.0.0.1` means “this same computer.” Later, when games use several JavaScript files, data files, or 3D models, a local server helps the browser load them safely. Starting one does not make your project public.

For now, opening `index.html` directly is enough. Learn the page's structure and style first; the next chapter does exactly that.

## Get ready for input and JavaScript

Web pages have **input elements** such as text boxes, checkboxes, menus, and buttons. In the next chapter, you will place them on a static site and label them clearly. They will be real browser controls, but they will not yet make a game remember a choice or react to a click.

That is intentional. First learn what HTML puts on a page and what CSS changes about its appearance. Then, in Chapter 3, JavaScript will find those elements and give them behavior.
